crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Retrieval-Grounded Legal Research
children.blurb: Retrieval-grounded legal research is the practice of answering a legal question by first pulling relevant authorities and documents from a defined corpus, then using a language model to summarize or draft from those sources with citations attached.

children.name: Adversarial Statutory Interpretation
children.blurb: Adversarial statutory interpretation is the practice of researching and arguing competing readings of a statute when parties have adverse legal interests.

children.name: Brief Drafting with Machine Assistance
children.blurb: Brief drafting with machine assistance covers the use of software to help produce legal briefs, motions, and memoranda for courts and clients.

children.name: Citation Auditing and Good Law Checking
children.blurb: Citation auditing and good law checking cover the verification of every authority cited in a brief, memo, opinion, or client advice, from case citations and pin cites to statutes, regulations, and secondary sources.

children.name: Jurisdictional Anomalies and Local Codes
children.blurb: Jurisdictional anomalies and local codes covers the places where AI rules do not line up: a state statute that conflicts with a city ordinance, a county procurement rule that reaches further than federal guidance, or a court rule that assumes a technology the local code never defines.

sections.body: Legal research and case strategy is the part of legal practice where a lawyer finds the governing authority, reads it against the other side's likely reading, and builds an argument that survives a judge. Artificial intelligence is now doing real work in each of those steps. Retrieval systems search case law, statutes and secondary sources and return passages tied to the query rather than a bare list of links. Drafting tools assemble argument sections from retrieved authority, and auditing tools check whether a cited case is still good law. The work is document heavy, text heavy and precedent bound, which is why it absorbed language models faster than many other professions.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Retrieval over a closed corpus works well when the corpus is clean and the citations are verifiable, and citation checking against a database is largely a solved mechanical task. What is not solved is the gap between fluent text and correct law. A model can produce a plausible sentence with a citation that does not exist or that no longer stands, and the failure looks identical to success until someone checks. Statutory reading across overlapping regimes remains hard because meaning depends on structure, definitions and history that retrieval alone does not capture. Local codes and jurisdictional quirks are the weakest area, since coverage is uneven and small jurisdictions are often absent from the underlying data. The honest limit is that these tools assist a lawyer who verifies, and they mislead anyone who does not.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here follow the order of actual legal work. Retrieval-Grounded Legal Research covers how a system finds authority and keeps its answers tied to sources, which is the foundation the rest depends on. Adversarial Statutory Interpretation takes that retrieved text and stress tests it against the reading an opponent will offer. Brief Drafting with Machine Assistance moves from analysis to product, covering how generated argument is assembled and where a human must intervene. Citation Auditing and Good Law Checking is the verification layer, confirming that every authority cited exists and still holds. Jurisdictional Anomalies and Local Codes handles the edges, the places where general rules break and local variation decides the outcome. A reader should start with retrieval, treat interpretation and drafting as the working core, and use auditing and the jurisdictional page as the checks that keep the output usable.
